exp3_5_1_titel: Class A: always current, lots of heat
exp3_5_1_frage: An amplifier plays a quiet tone. How much of the battery power reaches the loudspeaker as sound?
exp3_5_1_v1: Almost all of it. An amplifier wastes nothing.
exp3_5_1_v2: Only a small part. The rest turns into heat.
exp3_5_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_1_b1: IM1 shows about 0.1 A, even with no tone at all. The transistor gets hot.
exp3_5_1_b2: IM1 only shows current while a tone is playing.
exp3_5_1_s1: Put IM1 on A1 and A2. Connect +9V to A1.
exp3_5_1_s2: Put the 8.2 kΩ resistor on A2 and A3. Put the 100 µF electrolytic capacitor on B2 and B3, plus on B3. Connect A3 to B3 and G to B2.
exp3_5_1_s3: Put the NPN power transistor on A5, A6, B5 and B6: B on A5, C on A6. Connect A3 to A5 and A2 to A6.
exp3_5_1_s4: Connect B6 to LS1 and LS2 to B9. Connect B9 to 0V.
exp3_5_1_s5: Put one probe on C6 and one on C2. Connect B6 to C6 and B2 to C2. Switch on and look at IM1.
exp3_5_1_h1: Here the loudspeaker is the emitter resistor. A quiescent current always flows through it and the transistor.
exp3_5_1_h2: Calculate: battery power = 9 V times the current at IM1.
exp3_5_1_loesung: IM1 shows about 107 mA. So the battery delivers about 0.96 W. Only about 33 mW reach the loudspeaker as sound, that is 3 to 4 %. Almost 0.8 W heat up the transistor.
exp3_5_1_erklaerung: In class A, current always flows through the transistor, even without a tone. The tone only makes the current a little larger and smaller. This sounds clean, because the transistor never switches off. But the quiescent current costs power all the time. It turns into heat.
exp3_5_1_mehr: Here direct current also flows through the loudspeaker. Real loudspeakers do not like that: the cone is pushed to one side. Real class A amplifiers therefore block the direct current with a capacitor or a transformer. They have big heat sinks.
exp3_5_1_w1: Replace R1 with 10 kΩ. How do IM1 and the heat change? How does a loud tone sound?
exp3_5_1_w2: Set the generator to 2 V. What does the oscilloscope show at the output?
exp3_5_1_echt: Look at an old radio or amplifier. Can you see metal cooling fins? They carry away the heat of the output stage.
exp3_5_2_frage: Two transistors share the work: one for the upper half wave, one for the lower. What happens when the tone is very quiet?
exp3_5_2_v1: Nothing special. The tone sounds like class A.
exp3_5_2_v2: Very quiet tones fall into a gap. The tone sounds scratchy.
exp3_5_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_2_b1: At the output, a piece of the wave is missing at the zero crossing.
exp3_5_2_b2: The wave at the output looks exactly like the input.
exp3_5_2_b3: Without a tone, IM1 shows as much current as with a tone.
exp3_5_2_s1: Put IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put a 1 kΩ resistor on A2 and A3 and another on C3 and D3. Connect D3 to 0V.
exp3_5_2_s2: Connect A3 to B3 and B3 to C3. Put the 100 µF electrolytic capacitor on B2 and B3, plus on B3. Connect G to B2.
exp3_5_2_s3: Put the NPN power transistor on A5, A6, B5 and B6: B on A5, C on A6. Connect A3 to A5 and A2 to A6.
exp3_5_2_s4: Put the PNP power transistor on D5, D6, E5 and E6: B on D5, C on D6. Connect C3 to D5, D6 to 0V and B6 to E6.
exp3_5_2_s5: Put the 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor on B7 and B8, plus on B7. Connect B6 to B7, B8 to LS1, LS2 to B9 and B9 to 0V. Put probes on C7 and C2 and connect B7 to C7 and B2 to C2. Switch on.
exp3_5_2_h1: Compare the two curves on the oscilloscope. Look closely where the wave passes through the middle.
exp3_5_2_h2: A transistor only conducts from about 0.6 V between B and E. Below that, neither conducts.
exp3_5_2_loesung: With a tone, IM1 shows about 69 mA, without a tone only about 5 mA for the resistors. About 0.2 W reach the loudspeaker, around 32 %. At the zero crossing a piece is missing: crossover distortion.
exp3_5_2_erklaerung: In class B, each transistor works only one half wave. The NPN pushes, the PNP pulls. Without a tone neither conducts, so almost no current flows. That saves a lot of power. But each transistor needs about 0.6 V before it conducts. Around the middle there is a gap. There the wave is cut off.
exp3_5_2_mehr: The gap is called crossover distortion. With loud tones you hardly notice it, with quiet ones it sounds rough. Push-pull output stages have existed for over 70 years. That is why almost all pure class B stages were given a small bias.
exp3_5_2_w1: Set the generator to 0.5 V. Can you still hear something? What does the oscilloscope show?
exp3_5_2_w2: Switch the generator off. How much current does IM1 show now?
exp3_5_2_echt: Listen closely to a loudspeaker when a song fades out very quietly. A good amplifier still sounds clean then.
exp3_5_3_titel: Class AB: two diodes close the gap
exp3_5_3_frage: Two diodes give the transistors a small bias. Does the gap at the zero crossing disappear?
exp3_5_3_v1: No. The gap stays, diodes change nothing.
exp3_5_3_v2: Yes. Both transistors already conduct a little before the tone arrives.
exp3_5_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_3_b1: The wave at the output is round and without a gap.
exp3_5_3_b2: The gap is just as big as with class B.
exp3_5_3_b3: IM1 now shows no current at all.
exp3_5_3_s1: Put IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put a 1 kΩ resistor on A2 and A3 and another on C3 and D3. Connect D3 to 0V.
exp3_5_3_s2: Put one diode from A3 to B3 and one from B3 to C3, each with the ring pointing down. Put the 100 µF electrolytic capacitor on B2 and B3, plus on B3. Connect G to B2.
exp3_5_3_s3: Put the NPN power transistor on A5, A6, B5 and B6 (B on A5, C on A6) and the PNP power transistor on D5, D6, E5 and E6 (B on D5, C on D6). Connect A3 to A5, A2 to A6, C3 to D5, D6 to 0V and B6 to E6.
exp3_5_3_s4: Put the 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor on B7 and B8, plus on B7. Connect B6 to B7, B8 to LS1, LS2 to B9 and B9 to 0V. Put probes on C7 and C2 and connect B7 to C7 and B2 to C2. Switch on.
exp3_5_3_h1: Each diode has about 0.6 V across it. Together that is 1.2 V – exactly what the two transistors need to conduct.
exp3_5_3_h2: Switch the generator off for a moment and read IM1. That is the quiescent current.
exp3_5_3_loesung: The gap is gone. Without a tone about 28 mA of quiescent current flow, with a tone about 89 mA. About 0.26 W reach the loudspeaker, a good 32 % of the battery power.
exp3_5_3_erklaerung: The diodes hold both bases about 0.6 V away from the middle. So both transistors already conduct a little, even without a tone. When the wave comes, one of them takes over the current without a gap. That is class AB: a small quiescent current like class A, but thrifty like class B.
exp3_5_3_mehr: The diodes are made of the same silicon as the transistors. When the transistors get warm, they need less voltage. In real amplifiers the diodes therefore sit on the heat sink: they warm up too and lower the bias. Otherwise the quiescent current could keep rising.
exp3_5_3_w1: Take out one diode and replace it with a wire. What does the wave look like now?
exp3_5_3_w2: Compare the quiescent current with class A in 5.1. How much do you save?
exp3_5_3_echt: Almost every radio and small amplifier with transistors works in class AB. Look in a construction guide: often you see two diodes between the bases of the output stage.
exp3_5_4_frage: The amplifier plays loudly. Where does the power from the battery end up?
exp3_5_4_v1: All of it reaches the loudspeaker.
exp3_5_4_v2: Part goes to the loudspeaker, a large part turns into heat in the transistors.
exp3_5_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_4_b1: T1 and T2 get warm, even though the tone sounds good.
exp3_5_4_b3: IM1 shows less current than with a quiet tone.
exp3_5_4_s1: Build the class AB amplifier from 5.3. IM1 is on A1 and A2.
exp3_5_4_s2: Set the generator to 4 V. Switch on and read IM1.
exp3_5_4_s3: Calculate the battery power: 9 V times the current at IM1.
exp3_5_4_s4: Wait a little and see how warm T1 and T2 get.
exp3_5_4_h1: Power at the loudspeaker: the RMS current squared times 8 Ω.
exp3_5_4_h2: What does not reach the loudspeaker turns into heat – mainly in T1 and T2.
exp3_5_4_loesung: IM1 shows about 96 mA, so the battery delivers about 0.86 W. About 0.3 W reach the loudspeaker, a good third. T1 and T2 each take about 0.25 W and get warm. The rest heats the resistors and diodes.
exp3_5_4_erklaerung: A transistor in the output stage is like a valve. It lets through only as much current as the tone needs right now. The remaining voltage drops across it. Voltage times current at the transistor is heat. That is why output stages get warm, even when they sound good.
exp3_5_4_mehr: Class B is best when it is driven fully: then up to 78 % reach the loudspeaker. At half volume it is much less. Music is mostly quiet and only sometimes loud. That is why a push-pull amplifier is often below 50 % on average.
exp3_5_4_w1: Set the generator to 1 V. Calculate again: what percentage reaches the loudspeaker now?
exp3_5_4_w2: How much power does the quiescent current alone cost? Switch the generator off and calculate.
exp3_5_4_echt: Together with an adult, feel a battery loudspeaker after it has played loudly for a long time. Does the case get warm? That is where the amplifier sits.
exp3_5_5_titel: Class D: switching instead of braking
exp3_5_5_frage: Instead of braking the current, two MOSFETs switch fully on and fully off. Does that also produce so much heat?
exp3_5_5_v1: Yes. Switching makes things just as warm as braking.
exp3_5_5_v2: No. A switch is fully open or fully closed. Then almost no heat is produced.
exp3_5_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_5_b1: At the switching node the voltage jumps between 0 and 9 V. Still, a round tone reaches the loudspeaker.
exp3_5_5_b2: A loud square wave reaches the loudspeaker.
exp3_5_5_s1: The 555 is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to A2. Put the 470 µF electrolytic capacitor on A2 and B2, plus on A2, and connect B2 to 0V. Connect A2 to + (M8) and to R (M4) and − (M1) to 0V.
exp3_5_5_s2: Put 2.2 kΩ on A3 and A4 and 15 kΩ on A4 and A5. Connect A2 to A3 and A4 to DIS (M7). Put the 10 nF capacitor on A5 and B5. Connect B5 to 0V and A5 to THR (M6) and to TR (M2).
exp3_5_5_s3: Put the 10 µF electrolytic capacitor on C2 and C3, plus on C3. Connect G to C2 and C3 to CV (M5).
exp3_5_5_s4: Put the P-channel MOSFET on A7, A8, B7 and B8 (gate on A7, drain on A8) and the N-channel MOSFET on C7, C8, D7 and D8 (gate on C7, drain on C8). Connect the output (M3) to A7, A7 to C7, A2 to B7, D8 to 0V and A8 to C8.
exp3_5_5_s5: Put the choke on A9 and A10, the 22 µF electrolytic capacitor on A10 and B10 (plus on A10) and the 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor on C10 and D10 (plus on C10). Connect A8 to A9, B10 to 0V, A10 to C10, D10 to LS1, LS2 to E10 and E10 to 0V. Put probes on B9 and C9 and connect A8 to B9 and A10 to C9. Switch on.
exp3_5_5_h1: The 555 switches about 4500 times a second. The tone at the CV input makes the pulses longer or shorter.
exp3_5_5_h2: The choke and the 22 µF form a low-pass filter. It lets the average of the pulses through, but hardly the fast jumps.
exp3_5_5_loesung: About 0.27 W reach the loudspeaker. The MOSFETs together take only about 16 mW and stay cold. The whole circuit needs about 0.39 W, of which about 0.1 W is for the 555 alone. That is around 70 %.
exp3_5_5_erklaerung: A MOSFET that is fully on has hardly any voltage. One that is fully off has no current. In both cases voltage times current is almost zero. The pulse width carries the tone: long pulses raise the average, short ones lower it. The low-pass filter of choke and capacitor turns this back into a round wave.
exp3_5_5_mehr: Real class D amplifiers switch 300,000 times a second and more. Then tiny coils are enough, and you cannot hear the switching. Here it switches more slowly so that the app can calculate every pulse exactly. That is why you hear a faint high whistle. The control is also simple here: a 555 with the tone at the CV input also changes the frequency a little.
exp3_5_5_w1: Replace the 10 nF capacitor with 22 nF. How do the pulses and the whistle change?
exp3_5_5_w2: Take out the choke and replace it with a wire. What does the probe at C9 show?
exp3_5_5_echt: Small Bluetooth loudspeakers play for a long time on one battery. Inside there is almost always a class D amplifier. Look at the box: sometimes it says “Class D”.
exp3_5_6_frage: The loudspeaker should play about as loud as in 5.4. Can the class D amplifier do it with less than 50 mA from the battery?
exp3_5_6_v1: No. The same volume always needs the same current.
exp3_5_6_v2: Yes. Class D needs much less current for the same volume.
exp3_5_6_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_5_6_b1: IM1 shows about 44 mA – less than half of class AB.
exp3_5_6_b2: IM1 shows as much as with class AB.
exp3_5_6_b3: The tone is much quieter than in 5.4.
exp3_5_6_s1: Build the class D amplifier from 5.5. Put IM1 between +9V and A2: IM1 on A1 and A2, +9V to A1.
exp3_5_6_s2: Set the generator to 2.5 V. Switch on and read IM1.
exp3_5_6_s3: Goal: about as loud as in 5.4, but IM1 shows less than 50 mA.
exp3_5_6_s4: Try other generator voltages. Up to where does the current stay below 50 mA?
exp3_5_6_h1: When the tone gets louder, class D also needs more current. Find the point where both fit.
exp3_5_6_h2: The 555 and the 2.2 kΩ resistor alone already need about 11 mA.
exp3_5_6_loesung: At 2.5 V about 0.27 W reach the loudspeaker, almost as much as in 5.4. IM1 shows only about 44 mA instead of 96 mA. At 3 V it gets louder, but IM1 rises to about 70 mA.
exp3_5_6_erklaerung: Class D loses hardly any power in the MOSFETs. Most of what the battery delivers reaches the loudspeaker. Only the control with the 555 costs a fixed part. The louder the tone, the less this part matters.
exp3_5_6_mehr: A 9 V battery lasts about twice as long at 44 mA as at 96 mA. That is why class D amplifiers are in phones, headphones and battery loudspeakers. A CMOS 555 would need only about 0.1 mA instead of 6 mA. Then the circuit would be even more economical.
exp3_5_6_w1: Replace the 2.2 kΩ resistor with 4.7 kΩ. How do IM1 and the whistle change?
exp3_5_6_w2: Calculate: what percentage of the battery power reaches the loudspeaker at 2.5 V?
exp3_5_6_echt: At home, compare how long two battery devices play, for example an old radio and a small Bluetooth loudspeaker. Ask an adult which amplifier is inside.
lex_leistungstransistor: A power transistor works like a transistor, but it is stronger. It takes up to 1.5 A and, without a heat sink, about 1.2 W of heat. It amplifies about 120 times. There is an NPN type (printed LN) and a PNP type (printed LP). In output stages it drives the loudspeaker.
lex_mosfet: A MOSFET is a transistor controlled by a voltage. When the gate is more than about 2 V above the source, it conducts from drain to source. Then it is almost like a closed switch with 0.2 Ω. Almost no current flows into the gate. The N-channel type (MN) switches to 0V, the P-channel type (MP) to plus.
lex_drossel_1mh: This choke has 1 mH on a ferrite core and only 0.3 Ω. It takes 1.5 A. Together with a capacitor it forms a low-pass filter. It smooths the fast pulses of a class D output stage before they reach the loudspeaker.
exp3_6_1_frage: Two voltage dividers hang on the same battery. When does a meter between their middles show exactly 0 V?
exp3_6_1_v1: Never. There is always a voltage between two points.
exp3_6_1_v2: When both middles are at the same level. Then the bridge is balanced.
exp3_6_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_1_b1: With P1 in the middle, UM1 shows almost 0 V. When I turn P1, UM1 shows plus or minus.
exp3_6_1_b3: UM1 always shows 0 V, however P1 is set.
exp3_6_1_s1: Plug two 4.7 kΩ resistors into A1 and A2 and into A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp3_6_1_s2: That is the left divider. The knob P1 forms the right divider: connect A1 to P1a and P1b to A3.
exp3_6_1_s3: Plug the measuring point UM1 into B2 and C2, plus at B2. Connect P1s to B2 and A2 to C2.
exp3_6_1_s4: Switch on. Turn P1 all the way left and all the way right. Then find the setting where UM1 shows 0 V.
exp3_6_1_h1: A2 is the middle of the left divider. It is at 4.5 V. The wiper P1s is the middle of the right divider.
exp3_6_1_h2: UM1 measures the difference between the two middles. It is zero when P1s is also at 4.5 V.
exp3_6_1_loesung: With P1 in the middle, both middles are at about 4.5 V. UM1 shows 0 V: the bridge is balanced. All the way left or right, UM1 shows up to about 4.5 V, once plus, once minus.
exp3_6_1_erklaerung: A measuring bridge is made of two voltage dividers side by side. The meter sits across between them, like a bridge over a river. If both dividers split the same way, the voltage is zero. If one resistor changes just a little, the meter shows something at once. That is why bridges are used to measure tiny changes.
exp3_6_1_mehr: The battery voltage drops out at the zero: if it sinks, both middles sink the same, and the zero stays. The balance is as exact as the meter, not as the battery. The circuit is named after Charles Wheatstone, who made it known in the 19th century.
exp3_6_1_w1: Replace the lower resistor with 5.6 kΩ. Where is the zero of P1 now?
exp3_6_1_w2: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Does the zero stay in the same place?
exp3_6_1_echt: With two equal resistors, a potentiometer and a 4.5 V battery you can build the bridge for real. A meter between the middles shows the zero.
exp3_6_2_frage: Now a thermistor replaces one resistor in the bridge. At room temperature it is balanced. What does UM1 show when the hair dryer warms the thermistor?
exp3_6_2_v1: Nothing. The bridge stays at 0 V.
exp3_6_2_v2: UM1 shows a voltage. It gets bigger the warmer the thermistor gets.
exp3_6_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_2_b1: UM1 rises from 0 V to a few volts. Without the hair dryer it slowly goes back to 0 V.
exp3_6_2_s1: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and A2 and the thermistor into A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp3_6_2_s2: Connect A1 to P1a and P1b to A3. Plug UM1 into B2 and C2, plus at B2. Connect P1s to B2 and A2 to C2.
exp3_6_2_s3: Switch on. Turn P1 until UM1 shows 0 V. Now the bridge is balanced at room temperature.
exp3_6_2_s4: Put the hair dryer next to the thermistor (bar at the bottom) and switch it on. Watch UM1. Then switch the hair dryer off again.
exp3_6_2_h1: At 20 °C the thermistor has about 12.5 kΩ. When it gets warm, its resistance drops a lot.
exp3_6_2_h2: If the lower resistance in the divider drops, the voltage at A2 drops. The bridge is no longer balanced.
exp3_6_2_loesung: At 20 °C, A2 is at about 5 V. P1 is then at about 0.44. The hair dryer warms the thermistor to about 60 °C, and then it has only about 2.5 kΩ. A2 drops to about 1.8 V, and UM1 shows about 3.2 V.
exp3_6_2_erklaerung: The bridge only shows the change. At room temperature it is zero. Every degree more unbalances it a bit. So the temperature becomes a voltage that starts at zero. That is exactly what a thermometer needs.
exp3_6_2_mehr: A thermistor does not change its resistance evenly: a lot per degree in the cold, less in the warmth. Meters convert it with a table. Over small ranges, for example around body temperature, the curve is almost straight.
exp3_6_2_w1: Put the hair dryer one field further away. How big does UM1 get now?
exp3_6_2_w2: Swap the thermistor and the 10 kΩ resistor. Which way does UM1 point now?
exp3_6_2_echt: A digital fever thermometer has a tiny thermistor inside. It measures the warmth of your body.
exp3_6_3_frage: Inside the force sensor, four resistors sit on a metal beam. A weight bends the beam just a tiny bit. How big is the voltage that appears?
exp3_6_3_v1: Several volts, just like with a voltage divider.
exp3_6_3_v2: Only a few millivolts. You need an exact meter.
exp3_6_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_3_b1: Without a weight, UM1 shows 0 V. With 500 g it shows about 4.5 mV.
exp3_6_3_b3: With a weight, UM1 shows less than without.
exp3_6_3_s1: Plug the force sensor into A1, A2, B1 and B2: + into A1, − into A2, A+ into B1 and A− into B2.
exp3_6_3_s2: Connect +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V.
exp3_6_3_s3: Plug UM1 into C1 and C2, plus at C1. Connect B1 to C1 and B2 to C2. Switch on.
exp3_6_3_s4: Put the 500 g weight on the force sensor (bar at the bottom). Then add 200 g and 100 g.
exp3_6_3_h1: Inside, the force sensor is a measuring bridge of four resistors of 1 kΩ each. A+ and A− are its two middles.
exp3_6_3_h2: The weight stretches two resistors and squeezes two. They change by one thousandth per kilogram.
exp3_6_3_loesung: Without a weight UM1 shows 0 V. With 500 g it shows about 4.5 mV, with 800 g about 7.2 mV. That is about 9 mV per kilogram: 1 mV for every volt of the battery.
exp3_6_3_erklaerung: In the force sensor, strain gauges are glued onto a beam. They are thin metal tracks. When the beam bends, one track gets longer and thinner, and its resistance rises. Another is squeezed, and its resistance drops. All four are joined into a bridge. So the small changes add up.
exp3_6_3_mehr: The change is tiny: 1 kΩ grows by only 1 Ω at 1 kg. The beam gets about half a thousandth longer. It cannot take more than 2 kg; then it hits a stop.
exp3_6_3_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. What does UM1 show now with 500 g?
exp3_6_3_w2: Put on all three weights. Does the voltage match 800 g?
exp3_6_3_echt: A digital kitchen scale has a force sensor like this inside: a metal beam with strain gauges. See if you can spot it from below through a gap. Do not unscrew the scale to do this.
exp3_6_4_frage: The force sensor gives only a few millivolts. But both outputs are at about 4.5 V. Can an op amp amplify just the small difference?
exp3_6_4_v1: No. An op amp always amplifies the 4.5 V too.
exp3_6_4_v2: Yes. With four resistors it amplifies only the difference.
exp3_6_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_4_b1: Without a weight, UM1 shows 0 V. With 500 g it shows about 0.43 V.
exp3_6_4_b3: With a weight, UM1 shows less than without.
exp3_6_4_s1: Plug the force sensor into A1, A2, B1 and B2: + into A1, − into A2, A+ into B1 and A− into B2. Connect +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V.
exp3_6_4_s2: Battery 2 makes the negative voltage: connect +B2 to E4 and E4 to 0V. Connect −B2 to E5. E5 is now at −9 V.
exp3_6_4_s3: The op-amp module is already in the module bar. Connect A1 to + (M1) and E5 to − (M2).
exp3_6_4_s4: Plug 10 kΩ into C1 and C2 and 1 MΩ into C2 and C3. Connect B2 to C1, C2 to IN− (M4) and the output (M5) to C3.
exp3_6_4_s5: Plug 10 kΩ into D1 and D2 and 1 MΩ into D2 and D3. Connect B1 to D1, D2 to IN+ (M3) and D3 to 0V.
exp3_6_4_s6: Plug UM1 into C4 and C5, plus at C4. Connect C3 to C4 and C5 to 0V. Switch on and put the 500 g weight on the force sensor.
exp3_6_4_h1: 1 MΩ divided by 10 kΩ is 100. That is how strongly the circuit amplifies the difference between A+ and A−.
exp3_6_4_h2: The 4.5 V that are the same on both outputs cancel out. For that, both sides must be built the same.
exp3_6_4_loesung: With 500 g, UM1 shows about 0.43 V. The calculation would give 100 times 4.5 mV, so 0.45 V. Almost 5 % is missing: the 10 kΩ resistors load the bridge.
exp3_6_4_erklaerung: The differential amplifier amplifies only what is different at its two inputs. What is the same cancels out, here the 4.5 V. The op-amp module needs plus and minus for this: its output should start at 0 V and also be able to go below 0 V. That is why battery 2 helps.
exp3_6_4_mehr: Each half of the bridge has 500 Ω inside. They are in series with the 10 kΩ. So the circuit amplifies only about 95 times instead of 100 times. Bigger resistors make the error smaller, but then you would need huge feedback resistors. The next circuit solves this better.
exp3_6_4_w1: Put on all three weights. Work back from UM1 how heavy they are together.
exp3_6_4_w2: Swap the wires at B1 and B2. What does UM1 show now with 500 g?
exp3_6_4_echt: In every digital scale, an amplifier like this sits behind the force sensor. Usually it is packed into a small chip together with the converter for the digits.
exp3_6_5_frage: Three op amps are to amplify the force sensor together, and one knob is to set the gain. Do the three op amps load the bridge?
exp3_6_5_v1: Yes, even more than before. There are more resistors connected.
exp3_6_5_v2: No. The bridge goes straight to the IN+ inputs. Almost no current flows there.
exp3_6_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_5_b1: With 500 g, UM1 shows about 0.34 V. When I turn P1 to the left it gets more, to the right less.
exp3_6_5_b2: UM1 stays at 0 V, however P1 is set.
exp3_6_5_s1: Plug the force sensor into A1, A2, B1 and B2 as before. Connect +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V. Connect +B2 to E4, E4 to 0V and −B2 to E5.
exp3_6_5_s2: Three op-amp modules are in the module bar. Connect A1 to + (M1), + (M6) and + (M11). Connect E5 to − (M2), − (M7) and − (M12).
exp3_6_5_s3: First follower: connect B1 to IN+ (M3). Plug 10 kΩ into C1 and C2. Connect C1 to IN− (M4) and the output (M5) to C2.
exp3_6_5_s4: Second follower: connect B2 to IN+ (M8). Plug 10 kΩ into D1 and D2. Connect D1 to IN− (M9) and the output (M10) to D2.
exp3_6_5_s5: The knob goes between the followers: plug 1 kΩ into E1 and E2. Connect C1 to E1, E2 to P1a and P1s to D1.
exp3_6_5_s6: Difference stage: plug 10 kΩ into C5 and C6, 100 kΩ into C6 and C7, 10 kΩ into D5 and D6 and 100 kΩ into D6 and D7. Connect D2 to C5, C2 to D5, D7 to 0V, D6 to IN+ (M13), C6 to IN− (M14) and the output (M15) to C7. Plug UM1 into C8 and C9, plus at C8. Connect C7 to C8 and C9 to 0V. Put on the 500 g weight.
exp3_6_5_h1: The first two op amps amplify both outputs of the bridge. Their difference grows, the shared 4.5 V stay the same.
exp3_6_5_h2: Gain of the followers: 1 + 20 kΩ divided by (1 kΩ + part of P1). The difference stage amplifies another 10 times.
exp3_6_5_loesung: With P1 at 0.2 there are 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ = 3 kΩ between the followers. They amplify 1 + 20/3, about 7.7 times, the difference stage 10 times: 77 times in total. 4.5 mV becomes about 0.34 V. P1 all the way left: 210 times, P1 all the way right: almost 30 times.
exp3_6_5_erklaerung: The instrumentation amplifier takes the bridge voltage at the IN+ inputs. Almost no current flows there, so the bridge is not loaded. The two followers amplify the difference, but not the shared 4.5 V. A single resistor between them sets the gain. The difference stage turns this into a voltage against 0V.
exp3_6_5_mehr: Here the calculation is right: the error from the bridge has gone. Instrumentation amplifiers come ready-made as chips. There the resistors are matched very exactly, and only the gain resistor is outside. They work in scales, blood pressure monitors and devices that record the heartbeat.
exp3_6_5_w1: Turn P1 all the way left. How many volts does UM1 show now per 100 g?
exp3_6_5_w2: Put on only 100 g. Set P1 so that UM1 shows 0.10 V. Now 1 V means one kilogram. Check it with 500 g.
exp3_6_5_echt: A blood pressure monitor for the arm has a small pressure sensor. It is a measuring bridge too, and an instrumentation amplifier amplifies its signal.
exp3_6_6_frage: There are about 0.6 V across a diode when current flows through it. What happens to this voltage when the diode gets warm?
exp3_6_6_v1: It rises. Heat makes everything bigger.
exp3_6_6_v2: It drops, and quite evenly, by about 2 mV per degree.
exp3_6_6_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_6_b1: UM1 first shows about 0.59 V. With the hair dryer the voltage drops to about 0.51 V.
exp3_6_6_b2: With the hair dryer, UM1 rises.
exp3_6_6_s1: Plug the 8.2 kΩ resistor into A1 and A2 and the diode into A2 and A3, the stripe towards A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp3_6_6_s2: Plug UM1 into B2 and B3, plus at B2. Connect A2 to B2 and A3 to B3.
exp3_6_6_s3: Switch on. Write down the voltage at UM1. About 1 mA now flows through the diode.
exp3_6_6_s4: Put the hair dryer on the diode (bar at the bottom) and switch it on. Wait and watch UM1 and the temperature of the diode.
exp3_6_6_h1: The diode warms up slowly. After about 15 seconds it is almost as warm as the air from the hair dryer.
exp3_6_6_h2: Calculate: difference in voltage divided by difference in temperature.
exp3_6_6_loesung: At 20 °C, UM1 shows about 0.594 V. With the hair dryer the diode gets about 60 °C warm, and UM1 drops to about 0.513 V. That is 81 mV less for 40 degrees: about 2 mV per degree.
exp3_6_6_erklaerung: In a warm diode the atoms jiggle more, and more charge carriers break free. So the diode lets the same current through at a smaller voltage. At the same current, the voltage drops by about 2 mV per degree, almost evenly. So every diode becomes a thermometer.
exp3_6_6_mehr: From −20 °C to 120 °C the relation stays almost straight. That is why such a junction sits in many chips as a temperature sensor, for example in a computer's processor. A steady current matters: if the current changes, the voltage changes too.
exp3_6_6_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Is the voltage across the diode different? Does it still drop by about 2 mV per degree with the hair dryer?
exp3_6_6_w2: Put the hair dryer one field further away. Use UM1 to work out how warm the diode is now.
exp3_6_6_echt: Connect a diode with a 4.7 kΩ resistor to a 4.5 V battery and measure its voltage. Hold the diode between two fingers: the voltage drops by a few millivolts.
exp3_6_7_frage: Without a magnet, a Hall sensor gives half the battery voltage. What happens when a magnet lies on top of it?
exp3_6_7_v1: Nothing. Magnets only act on iron.
exp3_6_7_v2: The voltage changes: the south pole pushes it up, the north pole down.
exp3_6_7_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_7_b1: Without a magnet, UM1 shows about 2.25 V. With the south pole on top about 3.4 V, with the north pole about 1.1 V.
exp3_6_7_b3: UM1 shows the same with both poles.
exp3_6_7_s1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. The +9V socket now gives 4.5 V. Plug the Hall sensor into A1, A2 and A3: + into A1, − into A2 and the output into A3.
exp3_6_7_s2: Connect +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V.
exp3_6_7_s3: Plug UM1 into B3 and B4, plus at B3. Connect A3 to B3 and B4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp3_6_7_s4: Put the magnet on the Hall sensor (bar at the bottom). Tap the magnet to turn it over: S or N faces down. Also slide it slowly away.
exp3_6_7_h1: At 4.5 V the output changes by about 12.6 mV per millitesla.
exp3_6_7_h2: Right above the sensor the magnet has about 90 mT. Just one field further away there are only about 17 mT left.
exp3_6_7_loesung: Without a magnet, UM1 shows about 2.25 V, half the battery voltage. South pole down: about 3.4 V. North pole down: about 1.1 V. One field to the side, the voltage changes by only about 0.2 V.
exp3_6_7_erklaerung: In the Hall sensor, current flows through a thin plate. A magnetic field pushes the electrons to the side, so more gather on one side. Between the two sides a small voltage appears, the Hall voltage. An amplifier in the sensor turns it into a few volts. The direction of the field decides whether the voltage rises or drops.
exp3_6_7_mehr: Edwin Hall discovered this effect in 1879. Today Hall sensors count the turns of wheels, notice whether a phone case is closed, and measure large currents without touching. The field of a magnet gets weaker very quickly with distance.
exp3_6_7_w1: Slide the magnet away field by field and write down UM1. How quickly does the field get weaker?
exp3_6_7_w2: In the free lab, add a comparator with the op-amp module: with the south pole, an LED should light up.
exp3_6_7_echt: With a compass and a magnet you can see the direction of the field: the north end of the needle points to the south pole of the magnet.
exp3_6_8_titel: Project: scale with a light bar
exp3_6_8_frage: Force sensor and differential amplifier make a scale. Two comparators show: light, medium or heavy. From what weight does the green LED light up, and from what weight the red one?
exp3_6_8_v1: Both light up with very little weight.
exp3_6_8_v2: Green lights up from about 250 g, red only from about 560 g.
exp3_6_8_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_6_8_b1: Without a weight, no LED lights. With 500 g green lights, with 700 g green and red light.
exp3_6_8_s1: Build the differential amplifier from “Amplifying the difference”: force sensor into A1, A2, B1 and B2, +9V to A1, A2 to 0V, +B2 to E4, E4 to 0V and −B2 to E5. Plug 10 kΩ into C1 and C2, 1 MΩ into C2 and C3, 10 kΩ into D1 and D2 and 1 MΩ into D2 and D3.
exp3_6_8_s2: Connect A1 to + (M1) and E5 to − (M2). Connect B2 to C1, B1 to D1, D3 to 0V, D2 to IN+ (M3), C2 to IN− (M4) and the output (M5) to C3.
exp3_6_8_s3: The thresholds: plug 39 kΩ into A6 and A7, 1.2 kΩ into A7 and A8 and 1 kΩ into A8 and A9. Connect A1 to A6 and A9 to 0V.
exp3_6_8_s4: The comparators only need plus: connect 0V to E1. Connect A1 to + (M6) and + (M11) and E1 to − (M7) and − (M12).
exp3_6_8_s5: Green stage: connect C3 to IN+ (M8) and A8 to IN− (M9). Plug the green LED into C5 and C6, the long leg at C5, and 680 Ω into C6 and C7. Connect the output (M10) to C5 and C7 to 0V.
exp3_6_8_s6: Red stage: connect C3 to IN+ (M13) and A7 to IN− (M14). Plug the red LED into D5 and D6, the long leg at D5, and 680 Ω into D6 and D7. Connect the output (M15) to D5 and D7 to 0V.
exp3_6_8_s7: Switch on. Put the weights on the force sensor one after another: 100 g, 200 g, 500 g and also together.
exp3_6_8_h1: The amplifier gives about 0.86 V per kilogram. The thresholds are 0.22 V at A8 and 0.48 V at A7.
exp3_6_8_h2: A comparator is an op amp without feedback. If IN+ is higher than IN−, its output goes up and the LED lights.
exp3_6_8_loesung: Green lights from about 255 g (0.22 V), red from about 560 g (0.48 V). With 300 g or 500 g only green lights. With 600 g, 700 g or 800 g both light.
exp3_6_8_erklaerung: The scale has three parts: the sensor, the amplifier and the display. The display compares the voltage with fixed thresholds from a voltage divider. Each comparator is one step of the bar. The heavier the weight, the more steps light up.
exp3_6_8_mehr: The module bar holds three op-amp modules, so this bar has two steps. There are chips with ten comparators and a ready-made divider. They drive a bar of ten LEDs. A scale with digits turns the voltage into a number instead.
exp3_6_8_w1: Replace 1.2 kΩ with 2.2 kΩ. From what weight does red light up now?
exp3_6_8_w2: Set battery 1 to 4.5 V. Do the LEDs still light at the same weight? What changes at the sensor, what at the thresholds?
exp3_6_8_echt: Look at a luggage scale or a kitchen scale. Some show the weight with dots of light instead of digits. Inside it is the same: sensor, amplifier and display.
lex_kraftsensor: The force sensor (load cell) is a metal beam with four strain gauges. They form a measuring bridge of four resistors of 1 kΩ each. A weight bends the beam: two resistors get bigger, two get smaller. Between A+ and A− you get 1 mV per volt of battery and per kilogram. It can take up to 2 kg.
lex_hallsensor: The Hall sensor measures magnetic fields. It has three legs: +, − and the output. Without a magnet it gives half the battery voltage. A south pole raises the output, a north pole lowers it: at 5 V by about 14 mV per millitesla. It works from 3 to 6 V.
exp3_7_1_titel: When is a voltage a one?
exp3_7_1_frage: A computer only knows 0 and 1. But in a circuit there is every voltage between 0 V and 9 V. Which voltage is a 1?
exp3_7_1_v1: Only exactly 9 V. Everything else is a 0.
exp3_7_1_v2: High voltages are 1, low ones are 0. In between there is a range that is neither.
exp3_7_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_1_b1: Above about 6.3 V, LA1 shows H. Below about 2.7 V it shows L. In between it shows a question mark.
exp3_7_1_b3: LA1 jumps from L to H at exactly 4.5 V.
exp3_7_1_s1: Connect +9V to A1 and A1 to P1a. Connect P1b to E1 and E1 to 0V.
exp3_7_1_s2: Put the logic probe LA1 on B3. Connect P1s to B3.
exp3_7_1_s3: Put the measuring point UM1 on C3 and D3, plus on C3. Connect B3 to C3 and D3 to 0V.
exp3_7_1_s4: Switch on. Turn P1 slowly from fully left to fully right. Watch LA1 and UM1.
exp3_7_1_h1: The logic analyser at the bottom shows where H and L begin. The limits depend on the battery.
exp3_7_1_h2: With P1 in the middle there are 4.5 V. What does LA1 show then?
exp3_7_1_loesung: Up to about 2.7 V, LA1 shows L. From about 6.3 V it shows H. In the middle, for example at 4.5 V, there is a question mark. There the voltage is neither a 0 nor a 1.
exp3_7_1_erklaerung: In digital electronics a high voltage means H or 1 and a low one means L or 0. In between there is a forbidden range. Good circuits pass through it quickly. So a little noise does no harm: 8.5 V is still a 1, and 0.4 V is still a 0.
exp3_7_1_mehr: The limits of 70 % and 30 % of the supply come from CMOS chips. At 9 V they are 6.3 V and 2.7 V. Other chip families have other limits. The gap between the limits is called the noise margin.
exp3_7_1_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Where are the limits now?
exp3_7_1_w2: Use P1 to find exactly where the question mark begins. What does UM1 show?
exp3_7_1_echt: A logic tester for real circuits shows H and L with two LEDs. You can try it out with a voltage divider made of a potentiometer and a battery.
exp3_7_2_frage: A switch puts H or L on a transistor. What is at the collector then?
exp3_7_2_v1: The same as at the input: H stays H.
exp3_7_2_v2: The opposite: H becomes L, L becomes H.
exp3_7_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_2_b1: When W1 is at +9V, LA1 shows H and LA2 shows L. When W1 is at 0V, it is the other way round.
exp3_7_2_b2: LA1 and LA2 always show the same.
exp3_7_2_b3: LA2 always shows a question mark.
exp3_7_2_s1: Put the changeover switch W1 on A1, A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V. The middle A2 is the input.
exp3_7_2_s2: Put the transistor T1 on B3, B4, C3 and C4. Put 10 kΩ on B2 and B3 and connect A2 to B2.
exp3_7_2_s3: Connect C3 to 0V. Put 1 kΩ on B4 and B5 and connect +9V to B5. B4 is the output.
exp3_7_2_s4: Put LA1 on A2 and LA2 on B4. Put UM1 on D4 and D5, plus on D4. Connect B4 to D4 and D5 to 0V.
exp3_7_2_s5: Switch on. Set W1 to A1 (+9V) and then to A3 (0V). Compare LA1 and LA2.
exp3_7_2_h1: When the base gets current, the transistor conducts. Then it pulls the collector almost to 0V.
exp3_7_2_h2: Without base current the transistor blocks. Then the 1 kΩ resistor pulls the collector up to +9V.
exp3_7_2_loesung: When W1 is at +9V, T1 conducts. UM1 shows less than 0.3 V and LA2 shows L. When W1 is at 0V, T1 blocks. UM1 shows almost 9 V and LA2 shows H. The output is always the opposite of the input.
exp3_7_2_erklaerung: This circuit is called a NOT gate or inverter. It turns the level round: 1 becomes 0, 0 becomes 1. Here the transistor works as a switch. It is either fully on or fully off. That is why the output never lands in the forbidden range.
exp3_7_2_mehr: Around 1960 the first logic circuits were built from resistors and transistors. They were called RTL: resistor-transistor logic. Such a gate needs current even when it is idle. That is why today's chips use other transistors.
exp3_7_2_w1: Replace the 1 kΩ resistor with 10 kΩ. Does anything change at LA2?
exp3_7_2_w2: Connect the output B4 to a second inverter. What comes out then?
exp3_7_2_echt: With an NPN transistor, two resistors and an LED at the output you can build the inverter for real. The LED lights when the input is at 0.
exp3_7_3_frage: Two transistors sit one after the other between the output and 0V. Each has its own switch. When is the output L?
exp3_7_3_v1: When one of the two switches is at +9V.
exp3_7_3_v2: Only when both switches are at +9V.
exp3_7_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_3_b1: Only when LA1 and LA2 both show H does LA3 show L. In all other cases LA3 shows H.
exp3_7_3_b2: LA3 shows L as soon as one switch is at +9V.
exp3_7_3_s1: Put the changeover switches W1 on A1, A2, A3 and W2 on A5, A6, A7. Connect +9V to A1 and A5, and A3 and A7 to 0V.
exp3_7_3_s2: Put T1 on B3, B4, C3 and C4. Put 10 kΩ on B2 and B3 and connect A2 to B2.
exp3_7_3_s3: Put T2 on D3, D4, E3 and E4. Put 10 kΩ on D2 and D3 and connect A6 to D2.
exp3_7_3_s4: Connect the emitter of T1 (C3) to the collector of T2 (D4). Connect E3 to 0V.
exp3_7_3_s5: Put 1 kΩ on B4 and B5 and connect +9V to B5. Put LA1 on A2, LA2 on A6 and LA3 on B4. Put UM1 on C6 and C7, connect B4 to C6 and C7 to 0V.
exp3_7_3_s6: Switch on. Try all four positions of W1 and W2. Write down what LA3 shows.
exp3_7_3_h1: Current only flows when both transistors conduct. It is like two doors one behind the other.
exp3_7_3_h2: If even one of them blocks, the resistor pulls the output up to +9V.
exp3_7_3_loesung: When W1 and W2 are both at +9V, T1 and T2 conduct. UM1 shows less than 0.5 V and LA3 shows L. In the other three positions at least one transistor blocks, and LA3 shows H.
exp3_7_3_erklaerung: This is a NAND gate: NOT AND. The output is 0 only when both inputs are 1. The table with all four cases is called a truth table. You can build any other logic from NAND gates, even a whole computer.
exp3_7_3_mehr: The output voltage for L is a little higher here than with the inverter. Two conducting transistors drop more voltage than one. That is why you cannot put any number of transistors in a row.
exp3_7_3_w1: Put the two transistors side by side instead of one after the other. Which gate do you get?
exp3_7_3_w2: Connect an LED with 1 kΩ to the output. When does it light?
exp3_7_3_echt: Two NPN transistors, three resistors and two switches are enough for a real NAND gate. An LED at the output shows the result.
exp3_7_4_frage: The gate module contains four NAND gates. They work like your transistor circuit. When does an LED at output 1Y light?
exp3_7_4_v1: Only when both inputs are H.
exp3_7_4_v2: Always, except when both inputs are H.
exp3_7_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_4_b1: D1 lights in three positions. Only when W1 and W2 are both at +9V is D1 off.
exp3_7_4_b2: D1 only lights when both switches are at +9V.
exp3_7_4_s1: The gate module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp3_7_4_s2: Put W1 on A1, A2, A3 and W2 on A5, A6, A7. Connect +9V to A1 and A5, and A3 and A7 to 0V.
exp3_7_4_s3: Connect A2 to 1A (M3) and A6 to 1B (M4). Connect 1Y (M5) to C2.
exp3_7_4_s4: Put the red LED D1 on C2 and C3, plus on C2. Put 680 Ω on C3 and C4 and connect C4 to 0V. Put LA1 on A2, LA2 on A6 and LA3 on C2.
exp3_7_4_s5: Switch on. Try all four positions of W1 and W2.
exp3_7_4_h1: Compare with the last experiment. The module does the same as your two transistors.
exp3_7_4_h2: The output is only L when 1A and 1B are both H.
exp3_7_4_loesung: D1 lights as long as at least one switch is at 0V. When both are at +9V, D1 goes off. That is the truth table of the NAND gate.
exp3_7_4_erklaerung: A ready-made gate is easier to use than single transistors. Its output is strong: it can drive an LED directly. It sits almost exactly at +9V or at 0V. So one gate can drive another without the level getting worse.
exp3_7_4_mehr: The inputs of the module are Schmitt triggers. They switch to H only above 60 % of the supply and back to L only below 40 %. A slowly rising signal turns into a clean step. Real chips with four such gates have existed since the 1970s.
exp3_7_4_w1: Connect 1A and 1B together. What does the gate do now?
exp3_7_4_w2: Open »Look inside«. Where can you see the states of the inputs?
exp3_7_4_echt: A chip with four NAND gates is cheap and works from a 9 V battery. With two switches and an LED you can check its truth table for real.
exp3_7_5_frage: You only have NAND gates. How do you build a gate that lights only when both switches are at +9V?
exp3_7_5_v1: That is impossible. You need a different module for it.
exp3_7_5_v2: A second NAND turns the result of the first one round.
exp3_7_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_5_b1: D1 lights only when W1 and W2 are both at +9V. LA3 then shows L and LA4 shows H.
exp3_7_5_b3: D1 lights as soon as one switch is at +9V.
exp3_7_5_s1: The gate module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp3_7_5_s2: Put W1 on A1, A2, A3 and W2 on A5, A6, A7. Connect +9V to A1 and A5, and A3 and A7 to 0V. Connect A2 to 1A (M3) and A6 to 1B (M4).
exp3_7_5_s3: Connect 1Y (M5) to B9. Connect B9 to 2A (M6) and to 2B (M7). The second gate is now an inverter.
exp3_7_5_s4: Connect 2Y (M8) to C2. Put the green LED D1 on C2 and C3, plus on C2, and 680 Ω on C3 and C4. Connect C4 to 0V.
exp3_7_5_s5: Put LA1 on A2, LA2 on A6, LA3 on B9 and LA4 on C2. Switch on and try all four positions.
exp3_7_5_h1: A NAND with its two inputs joined is a NOT gate.
exp3_7_5_h2: NOT NAND is AND. Turning round twice gives the original.
exp3_7_5_loesung: The first gate gives NAND, the second turns it round. D1 lights only when W1 and W2 are both at +9V: that is an AND gate.
exp3_7_5_erklaerung: Every other gate can be built from NAND gates. NOT is a NAND with joined inputs. AND is a NAND followed by a NOT. OR comes out when you first turn both inputs round and then use a NAND.
exp3_7_5_mehr: Because NAND is enough for everything, it is called universal. Chip makers use this: a chip made of identical gates is easier to produce. The NOR gate is universal too.
exp3_7_5_w1: Build an OR: turn both inputs round with one NAND each and feed them into a third NAND.
exp3_7_5_w2: How many NANDs does an OR need? Is the module big enough?
exp3_7_5_echt: With a chip with four NAND gates you can build AND and OR for real. An LED at the output shows the result.
exp3_7_6_titel: A memory made of two gates
exp3_7_6_frage: Two NAND gates are cross-connected: the output of one goes to an input of the other. What happens when you press S1 briefly and let go?
exp3_7_6_v1: D1 lights only while you press S1.
exp3_7_6_v2: D1 goes on and stays on, even after you let go. Only S2 turns it off again.
exp3_7_6_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_6_b1: After pressing S1, D1 lights and stays on. Pressing S2 turns it off, and it stays off.
exp3_7_6_b3: D1 lights only while S1 is pressed.
exp3_7_6_s1: The gate module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp3_7_6_s2: Put 10 kΩ on A1 and A2 and the push button S1 on A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V. Connect A2 to 2A (M6).
exp3_7_6_s3: Put 10 kΩ on A5 and A6 and the push button S2 on A6 and A7. Connect +9V to A5 and A7 to 0V. Connect A6 to 1A (M3).
exp3_7_6_s4: Now crosswise: connect 2Y (M8) to C2 and C2 to 1B (M4). Connect 1Y (M5) to C9 and C9 to 2B (M7).
exp3_7_6_s5: Put D1 on C2 and C3, plus on C2, and 680 Ω on C3 and C4. Connect C4 to 0V. Put LA1 on A2, LA2 on A6, LA3 on C2 and LA4 on C9.
exp3_7_6_s6: Switch on. Press S1 briefly, then S2 briefly. Watch what D1 does after you let go.
exp3_7_6_h1: The two resistors keep 1A and 2A at H. A push button pulls its input briefly to L.
exp3_7_6_h2: An L at one input makes the output of that gate H. The other gate then holds it.
exp3_7_6_loesung: When you press S1, 2Y becomes H and D1 lights. The other gate gets this H and gives back L. So both hold each other, even when you let go of S1. Only S2 flips the circuit back.
exp3_7_6_erklaerung: This circuit is called an RS flip-flop. S stands for set, R for reset. It remembers one bit: on or off. That is the simplest form of memory. A computer's main memory holds billions of such cells.
exp3_7_6_mehr: When switched on, the circuit decides by itself which state it starts in. In real chips, tiny differences between the gates decide it. If you press S1 and S2 together, both outputs are H. That is not a useful state.
exp3_7_6_w1: Press S1 and S2 together and let go. What happens next?
exp3_7_6_w2: Connect a second LED to C9. What does it show?
exp3_7_6_echt: With a NAND chip, two push buttons and an LED you can build the flip-flop for real. It remembers the last button press until you take the battery off.
exp3_7_7_frage: You press a push button once. How often does the contact really switch?
exp3_7_7_v1: Exactly once. It is either open or closed.
exp3_7_7_v2: Several times within a few milliseconds. The contacts spring back.
exp3_7_7_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_7_b1: In the fine time window, LA1 and LA2 show several short jumps at each press. LA3 falls smoothly, and LA4 jumps only once.
exp3_7_7_b3: LA4 jumps as often as LA1.
exp3_7_7_s1: The gate module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp3_7_7_s2: Put 10 kΩ on A1 and A2 and the push button S1 on A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp3_7_7_s3: Connect A2 to 1A (M3) and to 1B (M4). Connect 1Y (M5) to B1. Put LA1 on A2 and LA2 on B1.
exp3_7_7_s4: Now the debouncing: connect A2 to C1. Put 100 kΩ on C1 and C2 and the capacitor 100 nF on C2 and C3. Connect C3 to 0V. Connect C2 to 2A (M6) and 2B (M7).
exp3_7_7_s5: Connect 2Y (M8) to D4. Put the green LED D1 on D4 and D5, plus on D4, and 680 Ω on D5 and D6. Connect D6 to 0V. Put LA3 on C2 and LA4 on D4.
exp3_7_7_s6: Switch on. Set the logic analyser to »fine«. Press S1 and let go. Take a freeze frame.
exp3_7_7_h1: In the coarse time window a bounce looks like a single jump. It lasts only about 3 ms.
exp3_7_7_h2: The capacitor can hardly charge in the short pauses. The Schmitt trigger only switches when it is right down.
exp3_7_7_loesung: When you press, LA1 jumps to L four times and back three times, all within about 3 ms. The capacitor at C2 discharges smoothly through 100 kΩ. After about 9 ms it falls below 40 %, and LA4 jumps to H exactly once.
exp3_7_7_erklaerung: Metal contacts spring back when they hit each other. For a lamp that does not matter. But a counter would count every jump. An RC network smooths the jumps, and the Schmitt trigger turns them back into a clean level. This is called debouncing.
exp3_7_7_mehr: Real push buttons usually bounce for 1 to 5 ms. The time constant of the debouncing should be longer, here 100 kΩ times 100 nF equals 10 ms. The resistor is large so that it hardly loads the button input. Many devices today debounce in software: they wait a few milliseconds after the first jump.
exp3_7_7_w1: Use a capacitor of 10 nF. Is that still enough for debouncing?
exp3_7_7_w2: Let go of the button. What does the bounce look like when it opens?
exp3_7_7_echt: With an oscilloscope you can see a real push button bounce. Connect the button with a resistor to a battery and measure the voltage.
exp3_7_8_frage: A door opens only briefly. How does the alarm system make sure that the light keeps blinking afterwards?
exp3_7_8_v1: It doesn't. The light blinks only while the door is open.
exp3_7_8_v2: A flip-flop remembers the alarm. A gate with a capacitor blinks as long as the flip-flop is set.
exp3_7_8_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_7_8_b1: After pressing S1, D1 blinks and does not stop. Only S2 resets the system.
exp3_7_8_b2: D1 lights all the time without blinking.
exp3_7_8_b3: D1 blinks only while S1 is pressed.
exp3_7_8_s1: The gate module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp3_7_8_s2: Build the flip-flop from »A memory made of two gates«: 10 kΩ on A1 and A2, push button S1 on A2 and A3, 10 kΩ on A5 and A6, push button S2 on A6 and A7. Connect +9V to A1 and A5, and A3 and A7 to 0V.
exp3_7_8_s3: Connect A2 to 2A (M6) and A6 to 1A (M3). Connect 2Y (M8) to C2 and C2 to 1B (M4). Connect 1Y (M5) to C9 and C9 to 2B (M7).
exp3_7_8_s4: The blinker: connect C2 to 3A (M9). Connect 3Y (M11) to D1. Put 100 kΩ on D1 and D2 and the electrolytic capacitor 10 µF on D2 and D3, plus on D2. Connect D3 to 0V and D2 to 3B (M10).
exp3_7_8_s5: Connect D1 to 4A (M12) and 4B (M13). Connect 4Y (M14) to E5. Put D1 on E5 and E6, plus on E5, and 680 Ω on E6 and E7. Connect E7 to 0V.
exp3_7_8_s6: Put UM1 on B8 and B9, plus on B8. Connect C2 to B8 and B9 to 0V. Put LA1 on A2, LA2 on C2, LA3 on D1 and LA4 on E5.
exp3_7_8_s7: Switch on. Press S1 briefly: the door opens. Wait. Then press S2.
exp3_7_8_h1: C2 is the output of the flip-flop. UM1 shows almost 9 V as soon as the alarm is stored.
exp3_7_8_h2: The third gate only oscillates when 3A is at H. The capacitor charges and discharges through 100 kΩ.
exp3_7_8_loesung: S1 sets the flip-flop: C2 goes to H and UM1 shows almost 9 V. Now the third gate oscillates with the capacitor about once per second. The fourth gate turns the level round and drives D1. Only S2 resets the flip-flop, and the blinking stops.
exp3_7_8_erklaerung: An alarm system has three parts: a sensor, a memory and a signal. The memory makes sure the alarm stays on, even when the door is closed again. The gate with a resistor and a capacitor is a clock. It flips every time the capacitor reaches a threshold of the Schmitt trigger.
exp3_7_8_mehr: The blink time follows from the thresholds: the capacitor swings between 40 % and 60 % of the supply. A whole period lasts about 0.8 times R times C, here around 0.8 s. With two gates you could also make a tone for a siren.
exp3_7_8_w1: Replace the 100 kΩ with 47 kΩ. How fast does D1 blink now?

exp3_8_8_mehr: How does a circuit calculate? The counter only counts one further. A computer can add two numbers, compare them and remember results – all with gates and flip-flops like these. You can discover that in Zuse 1.

exp3_0_2_b3: LA1 switches more often than LA2.
exp3_0_2_s1: Both 555 timers are already in the module bar. On both, connect +9V to + (M8) and to R (M4), and − (M1) to 0V.
exp3_0_2_s2: First clock: 10 kΩ on A1 and B1, 22 kΩ on B1 and C1, 10 µF electrolytic capacitor on C1 and D1, plus at C1. Connect +9V to A1 and D1 to 0V. Connect B1 to DIS (M7) and C1 to THR (M6) and TR (M2) of TI1.
exp3_0_2_s3: Second clock: 10 kΩ on A6 and B6, 10 kΩ on B6 and C6, 10 µF electrolytic capacitor on C6 and D6, plus at C6. Connect +9V to A6 and D6 to 0V. Connect B6 to DIS (M7) and C6 to THR (M6) and TR (M2) of TI2.
exp3_0_2_s4: Connect the output (M3) of TI1 to E1 and that of TI2 to E6. Put 680 Ω on E1 and E2 and the red LED D1 on E2 and E3, plus on E2. Put 680 Ω on E6 and E7 and the green D2 on E7 and E8, plus on E7. Connect E3 and E8 to 0V.
exp3_0_2_s5: Put logic probe LA1 on E1 and LA2 on E6. Switch on and compare the two rows.
exp3_0_2_h1: Each row in the logic analyser belongs to one logic probe. H is at the top, L at the bottom.
exp3_0_2_h2: In both rows, count how often the signal jumps from L to H.
exp3_0_2_loesung: The first clock runs at about 2.7 Hz, the second at about 4.8 Hz. So LA2 has almost twice as many edges.
exp3_0_2_erklaerung: An oscilloscope shows exactly how high a voltage is. In digital electronics, only one thing counts: H or L. That is why the logic analyser shows many signals one below the other, only as H and L. So you see at once which signal jumps when.
exp3_0_2_mehr: Real logic analysers have 8, 16 or more channels. They are used to find faults in computers where many lines switch at the same time.
exp3_0_2_w1: On the second clock, replace the 10 kΩ between B6 and C6 with 22 kΩ. What does the logic analyser show now?
exp3_0_2_w2: Set the logic analyser to »fine«. Can you see that an edge lasts only a very short time?
exp3_0_2_echt: You can build two 555 clocks with LEDs for real on a breadboard. They run on a 9 V battery.
exp3_0_3_frage: A square wave with 10,000 oscillations per second charges a capacitor. What does the voltage at the capacitor look like close up?
exp3_0_3_v1: The capacitor charges and discharges along a curve that you can only see when stretched.
exp3_0_3_v2: It jumps just like the square wave.
exp3_0_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_0_3_b1: Without the magnifier you see many narrow spikes. With magnifier ×10 you see one oscillation: the voltage rises along a curve and falls along a curve.
exp3_0_3_b2: Even with the magnifier the curve looks like a square wave.
exp3_0_3_b3: With the magnifier the screen is empty.
exp3_0_3_s1: Put 1 kΩ on A1 and A2. Connect G to A1.
exp3_0_3_s2: Put the 10 nF capacitor on C2 and C3. Connect A2 to C2 and C3 to 0V.
exp3_0_3_s3: Put probe K1 on C2 and K2 on A1. Switch on.
exp3_0_3_s4: The generator is set to 1 kHz. Set it to 10 kHz. The spikes get too close together to make out. At 10 kHz, »Done« turns green.
exp3_0_3_s5: On the oscilloscope, under »Time«, tap »Magnifier« until ×10 is shown. Now one box is only 10 µs wide.
exp3_0_3_h1: The magnifier stretches time: ×10 means you see everything ten times slower than it really is.
exp3_0_3_h2: Stretched pictures have a dashed frame and carry the magnifier sign with the factor.
exp3_0_3_loesung: With magnifier ×10 and 10 µs per box you see one whole oscillation. K2 jumps, K1 charges and discharges along a curve. After about one box the capacitor is almost two thirds charged.
exp3_0_3_erklaerung: Ten thousand oscillations per second are far too fast for the eye. The magnifier stretches the picture. To get it right, Volta then calculates in much finer steps. That takes longer, so with the magnifier the simulation runs slower than real – ten times slower with ×10. The time on the screen is still the real time.
exp3_0_3_mehr: The charging curve has a time constant τ = R · C, here 1 kΩ · 10 nF = 10 µs. After one time constant the capacitor is about 63 % charged, after five almost fully.
exp3_0_3_w1: Set the magnifier to ×100. How long is one box now?
exp3_0_3_w2: Replace 1 kΩ with 10 kΩ. Does the capacitor still get all the way up?
exp3_0_3_echt: Real oscilloscopes show very fast signals too, without any slow motion. For that they sample many million times per second.
lex_begriff_modulation: Modulation means: one signal rides on another. In a radio, the music changes a fast carrier wave. With AM its height changes, with FM its frequency. The receiver takes the music out again. This is called demodulation.
lex_begriff_resonanz: Resonance means: a tuned circuit swings along especially strongly at one particular frequency. That is its resonant frequency f₀. For a coil and a capacitor, f₀ = 1 : (2 · π · √(L · C)). This is how your radio picks a station.
lex_begriff_wirkungsgrad: Efficiency η tells you how much of the power you put in comes out as useful power: η = Pout : Pin. The rest turns into heat. A voltage regulator making 5 V from 9 V only reaches about 55 %. A switching converter often reaches 80 % and more.
lex_begriff_pegel: A level compares two voltages in decibels (dB). 20 dB more means ten times the voltage. 6 dB more is about twice as much. 3 dB less is about 71 %. In digital electronics, level also simply means H or L.
lex_begriff_flanke: An edge is the moment when a digital signal jumps. From L to H it is the rising edge, from H to L the falling edge. A counter counts on an edge, not for the whole time the signal is H.
lex_begriff_prellen: A push button does not close cleanly. Its contacts spring back and forth a few times before they settle. This takes only 1 to 3 ms. A counter sees several edges and counts too many. A capacitor or a Schmitt trigger smooths this out. This is called debouncing.
